claim: Cochlear implants are neuroprosthetic devices that can restore hearing in people with severe to profound hearing loss by electrically stimulating the auditory nerve.
source: Cochlear implants are neuroprosthetic devices that can restore hearing in people with severe to profound hearing loss by electrically stimulating the auditory nerve.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cochlear implants and their function.

claim: The acoustic information delivered by a cochlear implant does not convey the same level of acoustic detail as that conveyed by normal hearing due to physical limitations on the precision of electrical stimulation.
source: Because of physical limitations on the precision of this stimulation, the acoustic information delivered by a cochlear implant does not convey the same level of acoustic detail as that conveyed by normal hearing.
evidence: This statement references physical limitations including spatial spread of electrical current (Garcia et al., 2021) as cited support.

claim: Speech understanding in listeners with cochlear implants is typically poorer and more effortful than in listeners with normal hearing.
source: As a result, speech understanding in listeners with cochlear implants is typically poorer and more effortful than in listeners with normal hearing.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript (Firszt et al., 2004; Dwyer and Firszt, 2014) and established knowledge.

claim: The brain networks supporting speech understanding in listeners with cochlear implants are not well understood.
source: The brain networks supporting speech understanding in listeners with cochlear implants are not well understood, partly due to difficulties obtaining functional neuroimaging data in this population.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: High-density diffuse optical tomography (HD-DOT) is a quiet and non-invasive imaging modality with spatial resolution comparable to that of functional MRI.
source: using high-density diffuse optical tomography (HD-DOT), a quiet and non-invasive imaging modality with spatial resolution comparable to that of functional MRI.
evidence: This is a characterization of the HD-DOT imaging method based on established knowledge and prior validation studies.

claim: Listeners with cochlear implants showed greater activity in the left prefrontal cortex than listeners with normal hearing while listening to spoken words in quiet.
source: We found that while listening to spoken words in quiet, listeners with cochlear implants showed greater activity in the left prefrontal cortex than listeners with normal hearing, specifically in a region engaged in a separate spatial working memory task.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3, with statistical analysis showing t(27) = 2.3, p=0.015.

claim: The left prefrontal cortex region showing greater activity in CI users is engaged in a spatial working memory task.
source: We found that while listening to spoken words in quiet, listeners with cochlear implants showed greater activity in the left prefrontal cortex than listeners with normal hearing, specifically in a region engaged in a separate spatial working memory task.
evidence: This is supported by data from the spatial working memory task shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Listeners with cochlear implants require greater cognitive processing during speech understanding than listeners with normal hearing.
source: These results suggest that listeners with cochlear implants require greater cognitive processing during speech understanding than listeners with normal hearing, supported by compensatory recruitment of the left prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed increased PFC activity in CI users.

claim: The spatial spread of electrical current is a physical limitation on the precision of cochlear implant stimulation.
source: Because of physical limitations on the precision of this stimulation—including, for example, the spatial spread of electrical current (Garcia et al., 2021)—the auditory stimulation delivered by a CI does not convey the same level of acoustic detail as normal hearing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Garcia et al., 2021.

claim: Speech understanding in listeners with CIs is poorer than in listeners with normal hearing.
source: As a result, speech understanding in listeners with CIs is poorer than in listeners with normal hearing (Firszt et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Firszt et al., 2004.

claim: Even in quiet, listeners with CIs report increased effort during listening.
source: Notably, even in quiet, listeners with CIs report increased effort during listening (Dwyer and Firszt, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dwyer and Firszt, 2014.

claim: Many listeners with CIs attain significant success in understanding auditory speech.
source: Despite these challenges, many listeners with CIs attain significant success in understanding auditory speech.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cognitive demands increase when speech is acoustically challenging in listeners with normal hearing.
source: In listeners with normal hearing, cognitive demands increase when speech is acoustically challenging (Peelle, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peelle, 2018.

claim: Acoustically degraded speech can reduce later memory for what has been heard, even when speech is completely intelligible.
source: For example, even when speech is completely intelligible, acoustically degraded speech can reduce later memory for what has been heard (Cousins et al., 2013; Koeritzer et al., 2018; Rabbitt, 1968; Ward et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Cousins et al., 2013; Koeritzer et al., 2018; Rabbitt, 1968; Ward et al., 2016).

claim: To understand acoustically challenging speech, listeners need to engage domain-general cognitive resources during perception.
source: These findings suggest that to understand acoustically challenging speech, listeners need to engage domain-general cognitive resources during perception.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited memory studies.

claim: Even speech presented in quiet is degraded by the time it reaches the auditory system of a listener with a CI.
source: Importantly, even speech presented in quiet (i.e., without background noise) is degraded by the time it reaches the auditory system of a listener with a CI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical limitations of CIs discussed earlier.

claim: The cingulo-opercular network is engaged during particularly challenging speech.
source: The cingulo-opercular network, for example, is engaged during particularly challenging speech (Eckert et al., 2009; Vaden et al., 2017) and supports successful comprehension during difficult listening (Vaden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eckert et al., 2009 and Vaden et al., 2017.

claim: The cingulo-opercular network supports successful comprehension during difficult listening.
source: The cingulo-opercular network, for example, is engaged during particularly challenging speech (Eckert et al., 2009; Vaden et al., 2017) and supports successful comprehension during difficult listening (Vaden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vaden et al., 2013.

claim: Recruitment of prefrontal cortex varies parametrically with speech intelligibility.
source: Recruitment of prefrontal cortex (PFC) complements that in the cingulo-opercular network and varies parametrically with speech intelligibility (Davis and Johnsrude, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davis and Johnsrude, 2003.

claim: Activity in PFC, particularly dorsolateral regions, is associated with cognitive demands in a wide range of tasks.
source: Activity in PFC, particularly dorsolateral regions, is associated with cognitive demands in a wide range of tasks (Duncan, 2010), consistent with domain-general cognitive control (Braver, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duncan, 2010 and Braver, 2012.

claim: Functional MRI is not possible or subject to artifact in listeners with CIs due to the CI hardware.
source: Obtaining precise spatially localized images of regional brain activity has been difficult in listeners with CIs, given that functional MRI (fMRI) is not possible (or subject to artifact) due to the CI hardware.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of fMRI in CI users.

claim: Optical brain imaging has become a method of choice for studying functional activity in CI listeners.
source: Thus, optical brain imaging (Peelle, 2017) has become a method of choice for studying functional activity in CI listeners (Anderson et al., 2017; Lawler et al., 2015; Lawrence et al., 2018; Olds et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Peelle, 2017; Anderson et al., 2017; Lawler et al., 2015; Lawrence et al., 2018; Olds et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018).

claim: HD-DOT has been previously validated in speech studies in listeners with normal hearing.
source: In the current study, we use high-density diffuse optical tomography (HD-DOT) (Eggebrecht et al., 2014; Zeff et al., 2007), previously validated in speech studies in listeners with normal hearing (Hassanpour et al., 2015; Hassanpour et al., 2017; Schroeder et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to validation studies (Hassanpour et al., 2015; Hassanpour et al., 2017; Schroeder et al., 2020).

claim: HD-DOT provides high spatial resolution and homogenous sensitivity over a field of view that captures known speech-related brain regions.
source: HD-DOT provides high spatial resolution and homogenous sensitivity over a field of view that captures known speech-related brain regions (White and Culver, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White and Culver, 2010.

claim: The study examined brain regions supporting single word processing in listeners with a right unilateral CI relative to matched, normal-hearing controls.
source: We examine the brain regions supporting single word processing in listeners with a right unilateral CI relative to that in a group of matched, normal-hearing controls.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The multi-session analysis enabled localizing the left and right PFC based on the non-verbal spatial working memory task for one CI subject.
source: This multi-session analysis enabled localizing the left and right PFC based on the non-verbal spatial working memory task for this subject (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The multi-session analysis revealed the engagement of regions beyond the auditory cortex, including PFC, during the word perception task.
source: It also revealed the engagement of regions beyond the auditory cortex, including PFC, during the word perception task (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Strong bilateral superior temporal gyrus (STG) activations were found in controls during the single word presentation task.
source: We found strong bilateral superior temporal gyrus (STG) activations in controls similar to our previous studies using the same paradigm (Eggebrecht et al., 2014; Sherafati et al., 2020), as well as a strong left STG and a reduced right STG activation for the CI users (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and citations to previous studies.

claim: CI users showed strong left STG and reduced right STG activation during the single word presentation task.
source: We found strong bilateral superior temporal gyrus (STG) activations in controls similar to our previous studies using the same paradigm (Eggebrecht et al., 2014; Sherafati et al., 2020), as well as a strong left STG and a reduced right STG activation for the CI users (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Strong left-lateralized activations in regions beyond the auditory cortex, including parts of the PFC, were observed in the CI group.
source: In addition, we observed strong left-lateralized activations in regions beyond the auditory cortex, including parts of the PFC, in the CI group (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was a statistically significant difference between the control and CI groups in left PFC, t(27) = 2.3, p=0.015 (one-tailed).
source: Two sample t-statistics for the mean β values in each ROI support a statistically significant difference between the control and CI groups in left PFC, t(27) = 2.3, p=0.015 (one-tailed) and right auditory cortex, t(23) = 3.54, p=0.0017 (two-tailed) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a statistically significant difference between the control and CI groups in right auditory cortex, t(23) = 3.54, p=0.0017 (two-tailed).
source: Two sample t-statistics for the mean β values in each ROI support a statistically significant difference between the control and CI groups in left PFC, t(27) = 2.3, p=0.015 (one-tailed) and right auditory cortex, t(23) = 3.54, p=0.0017 (two-tailed) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The observed change in the left auditory cortex was not statistically significant, t(36) = 1.46, p=0.15 (two-tailed).
source: The observed change in the left auditory cortex was not statistically significant, t(36) = 1.46, p=0.15 (two-tailed).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Left PFC activation positively correlated with left ear unaided thresholds (p=0.01, Pearson r=0.55).
source: Using p<0.05 (uncorrected) as a statistical threshold, left PFC activation positively correlated with left ear unaided thresholds (p=0.01, Pearson r=0.55) and negatively correlated with right ear CI-aided thresholds (p=0.02, Pearson r=–0.49).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Left PFC activation negatively correlated with right ear CI-aided thresholds (p=0.02, Pearson r=–0.49).
source: Using p<0.05 (uncorrected) as a statistical threshold, left PFC activation positively correlated with left ear unaided thresholds (p=0.01, Pearson r=0.55) and negatively correlated with right ear CI-aided thresholds (p=0.02, Pearson r=–0.49).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Left PFC activation did not correlate with speech perception score (p=0.4, Pearson r=0.17).
source: Left PFC activation did not correlate with speech perception score (p=0.4, Pearson r=0.17) and aided hearing threshold for the left ear (p=0.1, Pearson r=0.36).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Left PFC activation did not correlate with aided hearing threshold for the left ear (p=0.1, Pearson r=0.36).
source: Left PFC activation did not correlate with speech perception score (p=0.4, Pearson r=0.17) and aided hearing threshold for the left ear (p=0.1, Pearson r=0.36).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: When listening to spoken words in quiet, listeners with normal hearing typically engage the left and right superior temporal cortex, including primary and secondary auditory regions.
source: When listening to spoken words in quiet, listeners with normal hearing typically engage the left and right superior temporal cortex, including primary and secondary auditory regions (Binder et al., 2000; Price et al., 1992; Rogers et al., 2020; Wiggins et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Binder et al., 2000; Price et al., 1992; Rogers et al., 2020; Wiggins et al., 2016).

claim: Prior studies have parametrically varied speech intelligibility and found intelligibility-dependent responses in the PFC.
source: Although we only tested a single level of speech difficulty (i.e., speech in quiet), prior studies have parametrically varied speech intelligibility and found intelligibility-dependent responses in the PFC.
evidence: This is a statement about prior research in the field.

claim: Use of several types of signal degradation revealed a classic 'inverted-U' shape response in the PFC as a function of speech intelligibility, with activity increasing until the speech became very challenging and then tapering off.
source: Use of several types of signal degradation (Davis and Johnsrude, 2003) revealed a classic 'inverted-U' shape response in the PFC as a function of speech intelligibility, with activity increasing until the speech became very challenging and then tapering off.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davis and Johnsrude, 2003.

claim: A similar inverted-U pattern was reported in functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS).
source: A similar pattern was reported in functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) (Lawrence et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lawrence et al., 2018.

claim: The region identified in left PFC is centered in left inferior frontal sulcus, extending into both dorsal IFG and inferior MFG.
source: This region was centered in inferior frontal sulcus, extending into both dorsal IFG and inferior MFG.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of the identified PFC region.

claim: The location of the identified PFC region is broadly consistent with domain-general ('multiple demand') activation.
source: The location is broadly consistent with domain-general ('multiple demand') activation (e.g., meta-analysis in Duncan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duncan, 2010.

claim: Reduced activity in the right auditory cortex in CI users relative to controls is attributed to differences in auditory stimulation.
source: We found reduced activity in the right auditory cortex in CI users relative to controls, which we attribute to differences in auditory stimulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data.

claim: Most CI subjects had poor hearing in their left ears, which would result in reduced auditory information being passed to the contralateral (right) auditory cortex.
source: Most of our subjects with CIs had poor hearing in their left ears, which would result in reduced auditory information being passed to the contralateral (right) auditory cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hearing data and known auditory pathway anatomy.

claim: Prior fNIRS studies have shown that activity in the superior temporal cortex corresponds with stimulation and comprehension.
source: Prior fNIRS studies have also shown that activity in the superior temporal cortex corresponds with stimulation and comprehension (Olds et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Olds et al., 2016 and Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: Activity in superior temporal cortex does not reflect only 'basic' auditory stimulation, but processing related to speech sounds, word meaning, and other levels of linguistic analysis.
source: First, activity in superior temporal cortex does not reflect only 'basic' auditory stimulation, but processing related to speech sounds, word meaning, and other levels of linguistic analysis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about auditory cortex function.

claim: The overall level of speech processing was significantly (p=0.00005) lower for CI users (mean speech perception score = 0.88, SD = 0.09) than controls (mean speech perception score = 0.99, SD = 0.01).
source: The overall level of speech processing was significantly (p=0.00005) lower for CI users than controls (mean speech perception score = 0.99, SD = 0.01), resulting in decreased activity (indeed, because the depth of HD-DOT includes only about 1 cm of the brain, much of primary auditory cortex is not present in our field of view, and the observed group differences were localized in non-primary regions of STG and MTG).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: The depth of HD-DOT includes only about 1 cm of the brain.
source: indeed, because the depth of HD-DOT includes only about 1 cm of the brain, much of primary auditory cortex is not present in our field of view, and the observed group differences were localized in non-primary regions of STG and MTG
evidence: This is a technical characteristic of the HD-DOT imaging method.

claim: Much of primary auditory cortex is not present in the HD-DOT field of view.
source: indeed, because the depth of HD-DOT includes only about 1 cm of the brain, much of primary auditory cortex is not present in our field of view, and the observed group differences were localized in non-primary regions of STG and MTG
evidence: This is an inference based on the depth limitation of HD-DOT and the anatomical location of primary auditory cortex.

claim: The observed group differences were localized in non-primary regions of STG and MTG.
source: indeed, because the depth of HD-DOT includes only about 1 cm of the brain, much of primary auditory cortex is not present in our field of view, and the observed group differences were localized in non-primary regions of STG and MTG
evidence: This is based on the data analysis and anatomical interpretation.

claim: Effortful listening depends on attention.
source: That is, given that effortful listening depends on attention (Wild et al., 2012), it might be that processes related to top-down prediction (Cope et al., 2017; Sohoglu et al., 2012; Sohoglu et al., 2014) are muted when too much cognitive control is required for perceptual analysis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wild et al., 2012.

claim: Processes related to top-down prediction might be muted when too much cognitive control is required for perceptual analysis.
source: That is, given that effortful listening depends on attention (Wild et al., 2012), it might be that processes related to top-down prediction (Cope et al., 2017; Sohoglu et al., 2012; Sohoglu et al., 2014) are muted when too much cognitive control is required for perceptual analysis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on cited work on top-down prediction.

claim: Poorer hearing in the left (non-CI) ear was correlated with increased activity in PFC.
source: Interestingly, we saw a trend such that poorer hearing in the left (non-CI) ear was correlated with increased activity in PFC.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Poorer hearing in the left ear would create a greater acoustic challenge, with a correspondingly greater drain on cognitive resources.
source: Thus, poorer hearing in the left ear would create a greater acoustic challenge, with a correspondingly greater drain on cognitive resources.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation data and cognitive load theory.

claim: fNIRS-based neuroimaging is an attractive method for studying the neural correlates of speech perception in CI users due to limitations of using fMRI and EEG.
source: Due to limitations of using fMRI and EEG in studying CI users, fNIRS-based neuroimaging is an attractive method for studying the neural correlates of speech perception in this population (Hassanpour et al., 2015; Lawler et al., 2015; Saliba et al., 2016; Sevy et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and established knowledge.

claim: Olds et al., 2016, showed that both normal hearing and CI users with good speech perception exhibited greater cortical activations to natural speech than to unintelligible speech.
source: For example, Olds et al., 2016, studied temporal lobe activity and showed that both normal hearing and CI users with good speech perception exhibited greater cortical activations to natural speech than to unintelligible speech.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olds et al., 2016.

claim: CI users with poor speech perception had large, indistinguishable cortical activations to all stimuli.
source: In contrast, CI users with poor speech perception had large, indistinguishable cortical activations to all stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olds et al., 2016 (implied from context).

claim: Zhou et al., 2018, found that regions of temporal and frontal cortex had significantly different mean activation levels in response to auditory speech in CI listeners compared with normal-hearing listeners.
source: Zhou et al., 2018, found that regions of temporal and frontal cortex had significantly different mean activation levels in response to auditory speech in CI listeners compared with normal-hearing listeners, and these activation levels were negatively correlated with CI users' auditory speech understanding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: Activation levels in temporal and frontal cortex were negatively correlated with CI users' auditory speech understanding.
source: Zhou et al., 2018, found that regions of temporal and frontal cortex had significantly different mean activation levels in response to auditory speech in CI listeners compared with normal-hearing listeners, and these activation levels were negatively correlated with CI users' auditory speech understanding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2018.

claim: The current study was able to simultaneously measure responses in temporal and frontal lobes with a high-density array.
source: Our current study differs in that we were able to simultaneously measure responses in temporal and frontal lobes with a high-density array.
evidence: This describes a methodological feature of the current study.

claim: The finding of increased recruitment of left PFC in CI listeners is broadly consistent with the recruitment of PFC in fNIRS studies in normal-hearing participants listening to simulated distorted speech.
source: Our finding of increased recruitment of left PFC in CI listeners is broadly consistent with the recruitment of PFC in fNIRS studies in normal-hearing participants listening to simulated distorted speech (Defenderfer et al., 2021; Lawrence et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Defenderfer et al., 2021 and Lawrence et al., 2018.

claim: This is the first fNIRS-based study to use a non-verbal spatial working memory task for localizing the PFC ROI in the same population.
source: To our knowledge, our study is the first fNIRS-based study to use a non-verbal spatial working memory task for localizing the PFC ROI in the same population, and it may be that increased use of cross-domain functional localizers will prove to be a useful approach in future work.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the methodological approach.

claim: The ability to image neural activity with fNIRS is limited by the placement of sources and detectors, and in depth to approximately 1 cm of the cortex.
source: As with all fNIRS-based functional brain imaging, our ability to image neural activity is limited by the placement of sources and detectors, and in depth to approximately 1 cm of the cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of fNIRS imaging.

claim: The HD-DOT cap covers the regions of superficial cortex commonly identified in fMRI studies of speech processing, including bilateral superior (STG) and middle temporal gyri (MTG), and pars triangularis of the left IFG.
source: Our HD-DOT cap covers the regions of superficial cortex commonly identified in fMRI studies of speech processing, including bilateral superior (STG) and middle temporal gyri (MTG), and pars triangularis of the left IFG (Davis and Johnsrude, 2003; Rodd et al., 2005; Rogers et al., 2020; Wild et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to fMRI studies and describes the coverage of the HD-DOT system.

claim: The HD-DOT cap has good coverage of occipital cortex and middle frontal gyrus.
source: We also have good coverage of occipital cortex and middle frontal gyrus.
evidence: This describes the coverage of the HD-DOT system.

claim: In the present study, pars opercularis of the IFG, the cerebellum, and subcortical structures were not imaged.
source: However, in the present study we do not image pars opercularis of the IFG, the cerebellum, or any subcortical structures.
evidence: This describes the limitations of the HD-DOT coverage in this study.

claim: The functional organization of the frontal cortex is complex and differs from person to person.
source: As we have pointed out, the functional organization of the frontal cortex is complex and differs from person to person; in particular, fMRI studies have demonstrated that regions responding to language and non-language tasks lie nearby each other (Fedorenko et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fedorenko et al., 2012 and established knowledge.

claim: fMRI studies have demonstrated that regions responding to language and non-language tasks lie nearby each other in frontal cortex.
source: As we have pointed out, the functional organization of the frontal cortex is complex and differs from person to person; in particular, fMRI studies have demonstrated that regions responding to language and non-language tasks lie nearby each other (Fedorenko et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fedorenko et al., 2012.

claim: Simulated CI speech (i.e., noise-vocoded speech) is associated with delayed word recognition.
source: Although we did not include an independent measure of cognitive challenge, we note that simulated CI speech (i.e., noise-vocoded speech) is associated with delayed word recognition (McMurray et al., 2017) and poorer memory for what has been heard (Ward et al., 2016), consistent with increased dependence on shared cognitive processes (Piquado et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMurray et al., 2017.

claim: Simulated CI speech is associated with poorer memory for what has been heard.
source: Although we did not include an independent measure of cognitive challenge, we note that simulated CI speech (i.e., noise-vocoded speech) is associated with delayed word recognition (McMurray et al., 2017) and poorer memory for what has been heard (Ward et al., 2016), consistent with increased dependence on shared cognitive processes (Piquado et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ward et al., 2016.

claim: Delayed word recognition and poorer memory for simulated CI speech is consistent with increased dependence on shared cognitive processes.
source: Although we did not include an independent measure of cognitive challenge, we note that simulated CI speech (i.e., noise-vocoded speech) is associated with delayed word recognition (McMurray et al., 2017) and poorer memory for what has been heard (Ward et al., 2016), consistent with increased dependence on shared cognitive processes (Piquado et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Piquado et al., 2010.

claim: Relating activity in PFC to cognitive demand is consistent with decreased activity in PFC when speech becomes unintelligible.
source: Relating activity in PFC to cognitive demand is also consistent with decreased activity in PFC when speech becomes unintelligible (Davis and Johnsrude, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Davis and Johnsrude, 2003.

claim: In the current study, only responses to speech in quiet were measured.
source: Finally, we emphasize that in the current study we only measured responses to speech in quiet.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study design.

claim: Everyday communication frequently occurs in the presence of background noise, which can be particularly challenging for many listeners with CIs.
source: Everyday communication frequently occurs in the presence of background noise, which can be particularly challenging for many listeners with CIs (Firszt et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Firszt et al., 2004 and established knowledge.

claim: Based on parametric modulations of acoustic challenge in listeners with normal hearing, increasing activity in PFC might be expected as speech gets more challenging, followed by cingulo-opercular activity once intelligibility is significantly hampered.
source: Based on parametric modulations of acoustic challenge in listeners with normal hearing, we might expect increasing activity in PFC as speech gets more challenging (Davis and Johnsrude, 2003), followed by cingulo-opercular activity once intelligibility is significantly hampered (Vaden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation based on cited prior work.

claim: 21 adult CI patients aged 26–79 years were recruited.
source: We recruited 21 adult CI patients aged 26–79 years (17 right-handed, 2 left-handed, 2 not available), and 19 age- and sex-matched controls (18 right-handed, 1 left-handed) (demographic information in Table 1).
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: 19 age- and sex-matched controls were recruited.
source: We recruited 21 adult CI patients aged 26–79 years (17 right-handed, 2 left-handed, 2 not available), and 19 age- and sex-matched controls (18 right-handed, 1 left-handed) (demographic information in Table 1).
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: One CI user was excluded due to poor signal quality.
source: We excluded one CI user due to poor signal quality (evaluated as mean band limited signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of all source-detectors) and one control due to excessive motion (see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria applied to the data.

claim: One control was excluded due to excessive motion.
source: We excluded one CI user due to poor signal quality (evaluated as mean band limited signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of all source-detectors) and one control due to excessive motion (see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria applied to the data.

claim: All CI patients had a unilateral right CI.
source: All CI patients had a unilateral right CI (manufacturer: 11 Cochlear, 6 Advanced Bionics, 3 Med-El).
evidence: This describes the CI patient characteristics.

claim: All subjects were native speakers of English with no self-reported history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
source: All subjects were native speakers of English with no self-reported history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for study participants.

claim: The HD-DOT system is comprised of 96 sources (LEDs, at both 750 and 850 nm) and 92 detectors (coupled to APDs).
source: Data were collected using a continuous-wave HD-DOT system comprised of 96 sources (LEDs, at both 750 and 850 nm) and 92 detectors (coupled to APDs, Hamamatsu C5460-01) to enable HbO and HbR spectroscopy (Figure 5; Eggebrecht et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the HD-DOT system.

claim: The HD-DOT system provides more than 1200 usable source-detector measurements per wavelength at a 10 Hz full-field frame rate.
source: The design of this HD-DOT system provides more than 1200 usable source-detector measurements per wavelength at a 10 Hz full-field frame rate.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the HD-DOT system.

claim: The HD-DOT system has been validated for successfully mapping cortical responses to language and naturalistic stimuli with comparable sensitivity and specificity to fMRI.
source: This system has been validated for successfully mapping cortical responses to language and naturalistic stimuli with comparable sensitivity and specificity to fMRI (Eggebrecht et al., 2014; Fishell et al., 2019; Hassanpour et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to validation studies.

claim: The auditory stimuli were presented through two speakers located approximately 150 cm away at about ±21° from the subjects' ears at a sound level of approximately 65 dBA.
source: The auditory stimuli were presented through two speakers located approximately 150 cm away at about ±21° from the subjects' ears at a sound level of approximately 65 dBA.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: The spoken word recognition paradigm consisted of six blocks of spoken words per run, with each block containing 15 s of spoken words (one word per second), followed by 15 s of silence.
source: The spoken word recognition paradigm consisted of six blocks of spoken words per run. Each block contained 15 s of spoken words (one word per second), followed by 15 s of silence.
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigm.

claim: Two runs were performed in each study session with a total of 180 words in about 6 min.
source: Two runs were performed in each study session with a total of 180 words in about 6 min (Figure 5A, middle panel).
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigm.

claim: The spoken word recognition task was first introduced by Petersen et al., 1988.
source: This task was first introduced by Petersen et al., 1988, and subsequently replicated in other studies with the same HD-DOT system used in this study (Eggebrecht et al., 2014; Fishell et al., 2019; Sherafati et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petersen et al., 1988.

claim: All sound files were generated from a list of short simple nouns (one to four syllables) pronounced with a female digital-voice audio using AT&T Natural Voices text-to-speech generator with the 'Lauren' digital voice.
source: All sound files were generated from a list of short simple nouns (one to four syllables) pronounced with a female digital-voice audio using AT&T Natural Voices text-to-speech generator with the 'Lauren' digital voice.
evidence: This describes the stimulus generation method.

claim: A spatial working memory task was adopted to aid in functionally localizing domain-general regions of PFC.
source: To better understand the left PFC activity we observed in our first few CI users, we adopted a spatial working memory task introduced in previous studies (Fedorenko et al., 2011; Fedorenko et al., 2013) in the remaining subjects to aid in functionally localizing domain-general regions of PFC.
evidence: This describes the rationale for including the spatial working memory task.

claim: In the spatial working memory task, subjects were asked to remember four locations (easy condition) or eight locations (hard condition) in a 3×4 grid.
source: In this spatial working memory task, subjects were asked to remember four locations (easy condition) or eight locations (hard condition) in a 3×4 grid, appearing one at a time.
evidence: This describes the spatial working memory task design.

claim: The spatial working memory task requires keeping sequences of elements in memory for a brief period and has been shown to activate PFC.
source: This task requires keeping sequences of elements in memory for a brief period and has been shown to activate PFC.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about working memory tasks.

claim: Each run for the spatial working memory task was about 8 min, with a total of 48 trials in the run.
source: Each run for the spatial working memory task was about 8 min, with a total of 48 trials in the run (Figure 5A, right panel).
evidence: This describes the spatial working memory task design.

claim: HD-DOT data were pre-processed using the NeuroDOT toolbox.
source: HD-DOT data were pre-processed using the NeuroDOT toolbox (Eggebrecht and Culver, 2019).
evidence: This describes the data processing method.

claim: Noisy measurements were empirically defined as those that had greater than 7.5% temporal standard deviation in the least noisy (lowest mean motion) 60 s of each run.
source: Noisy measurements were empirically defined as those that had greater than 7.5% temporal standard deviation in the least noisy (lowest mean motion) 60 s of each run (Eggebrecht et al., 2014; Sherafati et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the data quality criteria, supported by citations.

claim: The ΔHbO signal exhibits a higher contrast-to-noise ratio compared to ΔHbR or ΔHbT.
source: We only present the ΔHbO results in the main figures as we have found that the ΔHbO signal exhibits a higher contrast-to-noise ratio compared to ΔHbR or ΔHbT (Eggebrecht et al., 2014; Hassanpour et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eggebrecht et al., 2014 and Hassanpour et al., 2014.

claim: HD-DOT data were collected from nine subjects (four controls and five CI users in 13 sessions) using a spatial working memory task.
source: To accurately localize the elevated PFC activation in the CI group, we collected HD-DOT data from nine subjects (four controls and five CI users in 13 sessions) using a spatial working memory task (Fedorenko et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the data collection for the spatial working memory task.

claim: The visual spatial working memory task robustly activates PFC due to its working memory demands.
source: The visual spatial working memory task robustly activates PFC due to its working memory demands (and visual cortex because of its visual aspect).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about working memory tasks.

claim: The spatial working memory task shows activity that dissociates from nearby language-related activity.
source: Our logic is that in prior work this task shows activity that dissociates from nearby language-related activity (Fedorenko et al., 2012), and thus the region of PFC localized by this task is more likely to reflect domain-general processing (as opposed to language-specific processing).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fedorenko et al., 2012.

claim: The spatial working memory task shows strong bilateral visual and PFC activations.
source: Our results show strong bilateral visual and PFC activations in response to this task (Figure 6A left).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Speech perception accuracy was measured using two lists of AzBio sentences in quiet.
source: To measure auditory-only speech perception accuracy, we presented each participant with two lists of AzBio sentences in quiet (Spahr et al., 2012) (except one participant who only heard one set).
evidence: This describes the behavioral assessment method.

claim: Speech perception accuracy was calculated as the proportion of correctly repeated words across all sentences.
source: We calculated speech perception accuracy as the proportion of correctly repeated words across all sentences.
evidence: This describes the calculation method for speech perception accuracy.

claim: Hearing thresholds were summarized using a four-frequency pure-tone average (4fPTA), averaging thresholds at 500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz.
source: We summarized hearing thresholds using a four-frequency pure-tone average (4fPTA), averaging thresholds at 500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz.
evidence: This describes the method for summarizing hearing thresholds.

claim: For unaided testing, a value of 120 dB was assigned if there was no response at a given frequency.
source: For unaided testing, a value of 120 dB was assigned if there was no response at a given frequency; for aided or CI testing, a value of 75 dB was used.
evidence: This describes the data handling procedure for hearing thresholds.

claim: For aided or CI testing, a value of 75 dB was used if there was no response at a given frequency.
source: For unaided testing, a value of 120 dB was assigned if there was no response at a given frequency; for aided or CI testing, a value of 75 dB was used.
evidence: This describes the data handling procedure for hearing thresholds.

claim: Based on prior optical neuroimaging studies with similar speech-related tasks, 15–20 subjects per group would be sufficient to detect a moderate effect size.
source: Based on prior optical neuroimaging studies with similar speech-related tasks (Defenderfer et al., 2021; Eggebrecht et al., 2014; Hassanpour et al., 2015; Pollonini et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2018), we anticipated 15–20 subjects per group would be sufficient to detect a moderate effect size while also within our resource limitations.
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies and power considerations.

claim: A one-tailed two-sample t-test was performed for the main hypothesis of increased recruitment of PFC in CI users.
source: We performed a one-tailed two-sample t-test for our main hypothesis (increased recruitment of PFC in CI users), for which we had a strong directional hypothesis (greater activity in listeners with CIs than controls), and a two-tailed t-test for the left and right auditory cortex changes for which we did not have directional hypotheses.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis approach.

claim: A two-tailed t-test was performed for the left and right auditory cortex changes.
source: We performed a one-tailed two-sample t-test for our main hypothesis (increased recruitment of PFC in CI users), for which we had a strong directional hypothesis (greater activity in listeners with CIs than controls), and a two-tailed t-test for the left and right auditory cortex changes for which we did not have directional hypotheses.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis approach.

claim: Adjustments were made for unequal variances for left PFC and right auditory ROIs based on the significance of Levene's test.
source: We adjusted for unequal variances for left PFC and right auditory ROIs based on the significance of Levene's test.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis approach.
